title: How generative AI works: a working model
body_md:
## A face is not a signature

On a video call your project manager nods, says your name and leans back, exactly as always. Everything is right except the one thing a face cannot carry: permission to move the company’s money. An actor in a white coat can recite the anatomy of the knee and still cannot sign a prescription.

A generative model learns patterns from examples and, given a prompt, produces something new: text, sound, an image, a clip of video. A language model does it by predicting the next piece of text, again and again; image and audio systems use other methods to make their media. You need no internals to handle a suspicious request, only the difference between **appearance and authority**: a convincing sentence or a familiar face tells you little about who controls the account, the call or the payment instruction.

### What the tools change, and what they do not

A fraudster can pair public details with generated wording or media, so a detail can be accurate while the request is fraudulent. The reverse holds too: an honest person may use an AI writing tool, a translator, a bad connection or a video filter. So do not sort people by grammar, accent, fingers or lip movement. Such cues may make you look closer; they cannot vouch for anyone. Text detectors are shaky ground too: in NIST’s pilot their results varied widely with the system, and nothing there shows that one can be trusted on a single message. No fixed length of audio guarantees a voice clone or rules one out; quality depends on the tool and on the recording.

### Work back from the action

Say what the request wants changed: money sent, a code read out, bank details altered, a link opened, a secret kept. Then ask which independent route would confirm that very action. Open a contact or an app you already know, never a callback link or number the request supplies. When company funds are involved, follow the documented approval route even if the person is on video. A real account that has been compromised can send a fraudulent request too.

The method has limits. Verification fails if you take the number from the suspicious message, if an attacker controls several channels at once, or if the real person cannot be reached. In those cases stop the irreversible step and turn to another trusted contact, or to your organisation’s escalation procedure. Verification is a way of deciding, not a verdict on whether a file was generated.

### One minute

Name the requested action. Stop before money or credentials move. Leave the channel the request came in on. Confirm through a route you found yourself. Record the outcome if your workplace requires it. The same minute works against an ordinary impersonator as well as an AI-assisted one.

widget_config.goal: Tell a convincing look from verified authority before you act on a request.
widget_config.today_action: Write down one callback route you trust for a person or team whose urgent request might one day land on you.
widget_config.scope: General guidance for personal and workplace requests, checked 20 October 2026. Approval and emergency procedures differ from place to place. The people and calls in the cases are invented.

sources.title: FTC: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
sources.scope: US consumer advice, page dated September 2023: voice cloning, urgency, calling back on a number you know, and checking with another relative. The reporting route it gives applies only in the US.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US guidance on requests to transfer money or change account details: confirm through a second channel, and contact your bank at once if you suspect a transfer went to a fraudster. Company and national procedures differ.

sources.title: NIST: 2024 GenAI text-to-text pilot
sources.scope: Published June 2025. A benchmark built on machine-written and human-written summaries, where detector results varied from system to system. It does not show that a detector can be trusted on one individual message.

blocks.title: A flawless voice asks for a transfer
blocks.situation: A call comes in that sounds just like the treasurer. It asks you to send a supplier payment to a new account, and the office is closed for the night.
blocks.analysis: A matching voice and knowledge of the supplier can come from public or stolen material. The change of account is the real decision. Hold the payment, call the treasurer or the supplier on a number already on file, and then use the normal approval path.

blocks.title: A translated, awkward message is real
blocks.situation: A supplier you have dealt with for years emails in oddly formal English, clearly run through a translation app, to say a pallet is delayed. All the message asks is that you read the delay notice already posted in the supplier portal you normally use.
blocks.analysis: Awkward wording does not make a message fraudulent. Open the portal yourself and read the notice. Do not accuse the supplier, and do not treat an AI-text score as proof of who is writing.

blocks.title: The convincing video request
blocks.setup: An invented scene: a project manager appears on a video call about a rush payment to a vendor, and the same request has arrived in chat. Each decision is a separate snapshot; nothing you do in one carries into the next. No real accounts or payments are involved.

steps.prompt: The face and the voice both match. What do you weigh first?

choices.text: Whether the video shows a lip-sync error
choices.consequence: You see no flaw, and the pressure to transfer is still there.
choices.explanation: Clean video does not prove who is running the meeting.

choices.text: The requested change to the payment details
choices.consequence: You name the irreversible step before you trust the presentation.
choices.explanation: The risk lies in approving a new destination for the money; the media only delivers the request.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: the manager posts a callback number in the chat. Which route do you take?

choices.text: The manager’s number in the existing staff directory
choices.consequence: You step out of a thread an attacker may control.
choices.explanation: A contact stored independently is a separate check; a pasted number belongs to the request.

choices.text: The new number, because it is faster
choices.consequence: The same person can pick up and repeat the story.
choices.explanation: A second medium is not independent when its address came from the first.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: you ring the manager on the number in the existing staff directory and nobody answers. The deadline for the new-account payment is close. What now?

choices.text: Approve it; the video looked normal
choices.consequence: In this scene the money lands in the unverified new account.
choices.explanation: Appearance cannot stand in for approval. Retry the decision by the existing route.

choices.text: Pause the payment and escalate to the usual approver
choices.consequence: The payment waits while someone authorised checks it.
choices.explanation: An unanswered callback is not an approval; the established controls still apply.

blocks.debrief: The thing to catch was the change of payment details. AI may or may not have been involved, and you never had to prove it to protect the transaction. Retry any decision and watch the result change.

questions.prompt: A real account sends an odd request to add a new beneficiary. What matters?

choices.text: Check the account change through the established process
choices.explanation: A real account can be compromised; a high-risk action still needs independent approval.

choices.text: Trust it, because the account is genuine
choices.explanation: Owning the account does not prove that this particular message is authorised.

questions.prompt: An odd accent turns up on a call that asks for no money. What does it prove?

choices.text: That the speaker is a clone
choices.explanation: An accent alone is not a reliable deepfake test.

choices.text: Nothing decisive about who they are
choices.explanation: Connection quality, translation and ordinary individual variation all change how a voice sounds.

questions.prompt: The caller gives you a second phone number so you can verify them. Is that independent?

choices.text: No; find a number you already have stored
choices.explanation: The attacker can control the call and the number they have just supplied.

choices.text: Yes; two numbers always establish identity
choices.explanation: Different numbers are not independent when both arrived with the same request.
